claim: Plant genomes encode hundreds of secreted peptides.
source: Plant genomes encode hundreds of secreted peptides; however, relatively few have been characterised.
evidence: This is a general statement about plant genomes that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Relatively few secreted peptides have been characterised.
source: Plant genomes encode hundreds of secreted peptides; however, relatively few have been characterised.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as established in the literature.

claim: CTNIPs are an uncharacterised, stress-induced family of plant signalling peptides.
source: We report here an uncharacterised, stress-induced family of plant signalling peptides, which we call CTNIPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing stress-induced expression and signaling activity of CTNIPs presented in the manuscript.

claim: BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1-ASSOCIATED KINASE 1 (BAK1) is a common co-receptor involved in CTNIP-induced responses.
source: Based on the role of the common co-receptor BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1-ASSOCIATED KINASE 1 (BAK1) in CTNIP-induced responses, we identified in Arabidopsis thaliana the orphan receptor kinase HAESA-LIKE 3 (HSL3) as the CTNIP receptor via a proteomics approach.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing BAK1's involvement in CTNIP signaling presented in the manuscript.

claim: HSL3 is the CTNIP receptor in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Based on the role of the common co-receptor BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1-ASSOCIATED KINASE 1 (BAK1) in CTNIP-induced responses, we identified in Arabidopsis thaliana the orphan receptor kinase HAESA-LIKE 3 (HSL3) as the CTNIP receptor via a proteomics approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data and multiple biochemical and genetic experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: HSL3 was identified as the CTNIP receptor via a proteomics approach.
source: Based on the role of the common co-receptor BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1-ASSOCIATED KINASE 1 (BAK1) in CTNIP-induced responses, we identified in Arabidopsis thaliana the orphan receptor kinase HAESA-LIKE 3 (HSL3) as the CTNIP receptor via a proteomics approach.
evidence: The manuscript describes mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiments used to identify HSL3.

claim: CTNIP-binding involves HSL3.
source: CTNIP-binding, ligand-triggered complex formation with BAK1, and induced downstream responses all involve HSL3.
evidence: This is supported by isothermal titration calorimetry data showing direct binding between CTNIP and HSL3.

claim: Ligand-triggered complex formation with BAK1 involves HSL3.
source: CTNIP-binding, ligand-triggered complex formation with BAK1, and induced downstream responses all involve HSL3.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and ITC data showing CTNIP-induced HSL3-BAK1 complex formation.

claim: CTNIP-induced downstream responses involve HSL3.
source: CTNIP-binding, ligand-triggered complex formation with BAK1, and induced downstream responses all involve HSL3.
evidence: This is supported by genetic data showing loss of CTNIP responses in hsl3 mutants.

claim: The HSL3-CTNIP signalling module is evolutionarily conserved amongst most extant angiosperms.
source: Notably, the HSL3-CTNIP signalling module is evolutionarily conserved amongst most extant angiosperms.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing conservation of both HSL3 and CTNIPs across angiosperm species.

claim: Secreted plant signalling peptides play major roles in growth, development, and stress responses.
source: Secreted plant signalling peptides play major roles in growth, development, and stress responses (Olsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Many hundreds of signalling peptides are predicted to be encoded in plant genomes.
source: Whilst many hundreds of signalling peptides are predicted to be encoded in plant genomes, relatively few have been characterised and their corresponding receptors are mostly unknown (Boschiero et al., 2020; Ghorbani et al., 2015; Olsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The corresponding receptors for most signalling peptides are mostly unknown.
source: Whilst many hundreds of signalling peptides are predicted to be encoded in plant genomes, relatively few have been characterised and their corresponding receptors are mostly unknown (Boschiero et al., 2020; Ghorbani et al., 2015; Olsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most signalling peptides are recognised by cell-surface localised receptors, especially by leucine-rich repeat receptor kinases (LRR-RKs).
source: Most signalling peptides are recognised by cell-surface localised receptors, especially by leucine-rich repeat receptor kinases (LRR-RKs).
evidence: This is a general statement about peptide recognition that draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: LRR-RKs generally function through the ligand-dependent recruitment of a shape complementary co-receptor to form an active signalling complex.
source: LRR-RKs generally function through the ligand-dependent recruitment of a shape complementary co-receptor to form an active signalling complex (Hohmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The best characterised peptide receptors belong to LRR-RK subfamily XI.
source: The best characterised peptide receptors belong to LRR-RK subfamily XI, these receptors recognise distinct families of plant peptides involved in growth, development, or stress responses (Furumizu et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: LRR-RK subfamily XI receptors recognise distinct families of plant peptides involved in growth, development, or stress responses.
source: The best characterised peptide receptors belong to LRR-RK subfamily XI, these receptors recognise distinct families of plant peptides involved in growth, development, or stress responses (Furumizu et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MIK2 belongs to the closely related LRR-RK subfamily XIIb.
source: Notably, the LRR-RK MIK2, which belongs to the closely related LRR-RK subfamily XIIb (an outgroup recently included within subfamily XI; Liu et al., 2017; Man et al., 2020) was recently shown to perceive SCOOP peptides (Hou et al., 2021; Rhodes et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LRR-RK subfamily XIIb is an outgroup recently included within subfamily XI.
source: Notably, the LRR-RK MIK2, which belongs to the closely related LRR-RK subfamily XIIb (an outgroup recently included within subfamily XI; Liu et al., 2017; Man et al., 2020) was recently shown to perceive SCOOP peptides (Hou et al., 2021; Rhodes et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MIK2 was recently shown to perceive SCOOP peptides.
source: Notably, the LRR-RK MIK2, which belongs to the closely related LRR-RK subfamily XIIb (an outgroup recently included within subfamily XI; Liu et al., 2017; Man et al., 2020) was recently shown to perceive SCOOP peptides (Hou et al., 2021; Rhodes et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ligand for HAESA-like 3 (HSL3) has remained elusive.
source: Despite intensive studies on the LRR-RK subfamily XI, the ligand for HAESA-like 3 (HSL3) has remained elusive, hindering our ability to investigate peptide-receptor co-evolution across the family (Furumizu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature and represents the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The unknown ligand for HSL3 has hindered the ability to investigate peptide-receptor co-evolution across the LRR-RK subfamily XI family.
source: Despite intensive studies on the LRR-RK subfamily XI, the ligand for HAESA-like 3 (HSL3) has remained elusive, hindering our ability to investigate peptide-receptor co-evolution across the family (Furumizu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the lack of ligand information cited in the literature.

claim: Several peptides (PEPs, PIPs, SCOOPs, CLEs, and IDLs) recognised by LRR-RKs from subfamily XI or XIIb are transcriptionally up-regulated by abiotic or biotic stresses.
source: Several peptides (PEPs, PIPs, SCOOPs, CLEs, and IDLs) recognised by LRR-RKs from subfamily XI or XIIb are transcriptionally up-regulated by abiotic or biotic stresses (Bartels et al., 2013; Gully et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2021; Takahashi et al., 2018; Vie et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: CTNIP1-4 transcripts are induced upon biotic elicitor treatment.
source: In order to identify novel stress-induced signalling peptides, we searched for Arabidopsis thaliana (hereafter, Arabidopsis) transcripts encoding short proteins (<150 amino acids) with a predicted signal peptide, which were induced upon biotic elicitor treatment (Supplementary file 1; Bjornson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data from Bjornson et al., 2021 showing upregulation of CTNIP transcripts.

claim: CTNIPs are a family of peptides with five predicted members in Arabidopsis.
source: Through this analysis, we identified an uncharacterised family of peptides with five predicted members, which we named CTNIP1–5 (pronounced catnip; AT1G06135, AT1G06137, AT2G31335, AT2G31345, and AT3G23123, respectively) based on relatively conserved residues within the peptides (Figure 1a–b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and sequence data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CTNIPs were named based on relatively conserved residues within the peptides.
source: Through this analysis, we identified an uncharacterised family of peptides with five predicted members, which we named CTNIP1–5 (pronounced catnip; AT1G06135, AT1G06137, AT2G31335, AT2G31345, and AT3G23123, respectively) based on relatively conserved residues within the peptides (Figure 1a–b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data shown in the figures.

claim: CTNIP1-4 peptides induce cytoplasmic Ca2+ influx.
source: CTNIP1–4 peptides were able to induce cytoplasmic Ca2+ influx and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation – hallmarks of peptide signalling (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from aequorin-based calcium measurements shown in Figure 1c-d.

claim: CTNIP1-4 peptides induce mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation.
source: CTNIP1–4 peptides were able to induce cytoplasmic Ca2+ influx and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation – hallmarks of peptide signalling (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing MAPK phosphorylation in Figure 1e.

claim: Cytoplasmic Ca2+ influx and MAPK phosphorylation are hallmarks of peptide signalling.
source: CTNIP1–4 peptides were able to induce cytoplasmic Ca2+ influx and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation – hallmarks of peptide signalling (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of plant peptide signaling.

claim: A synthetic peptide derived from CTNIP5 was inactive.
source: However, a synthetic peptide derived from the divergent CTNIP5 peptide was inactive (Figure 1—figure supplements 1a and 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no calcium influx in response to CTNIP5 treatment.

claim: The C-terminal 23 amino acids of CTNIP4 (CTNIP448-70) are sufficient to induce responses.
source: Notably, the C-terminal 23 amino acids of CTNIP4 (CTNIP448-70) were sufficient to induce responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b), suggesting that the minimal bioactive peptide is contained within this region.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing MAPK phosphorylation in response to CTNIP448-70.

claim: The minimal bioactive peptide of CTNIP4 is contained within the C-terminal 23 amino acids.
source: Notably, the C-terminal 23 amino acids of CTNIP4 (CTNIP448-70) were sufficient to induce responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b), suggesting that the minimal bioactive peptide is contained within this region.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CTNIP448-70 is sufficient for activity.

claim: The C-terminal 23 amino acids of CTNIP4 contain two highly conserved cysteine residues.
source: Notably, this region contains two highly conserved cysteine residues (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1b.

claim: The two conserved cysteine residues in CTNIP4 are required for CTNIP4 activity.
source: Mutation of these cysteine residues revealed they are required for CTNIP4 activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing loss of calcium influx when cysteines are mutated.

claim: CTNIP4 transcript was the most up-regulated upon elicitor treatment among the CTNIP family members.
source: Going forward, we focused on CTNIP4 as a representative member of this peptide family, as its transcript was the most up-regulated upon elicitor treatment (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is shown in the expression heatmap in Figure 1a.

claim: CTNIPs may be perceived by a cell-surface LRR-receptor.
source: We hypothesised that CTNIPs may be perceived by a cell-surface LRR-receptor.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known mechanisms of peptide perception and the characteristics of CTNIPs.

claim: LRR-receptors are typically dependent upon the SOMATIC EMBRYOGENESIS RECEPTOR KINASE (SERK) family of co-receptors.
source: Typically LRR-receptors are dependent upon the SOMATIC EMBRYOGENESIS RECEPTOR KINASE (SERK) family of co-receptors (Hohmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: CTNIP4-induced ROS production is significantly impaired in bak1-5.
source: Concordant with perception by an LRR-receptor, we observed significantly impaired CTNIP4-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in bak1-5 (Figure 1f–g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced ROS production in bak1-5 mutants in Figure 1f-g.

claim: Ligand binding induces receptor-SERK heterodimerisation to activate signalling.
source: Ligand binding induces receptor-SERK heterodimerisation to activate signalling (Hohmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: HSL3 was the protein most enriched in the BAK1 complex upon CTNIP4 treatment in four independent biological replicates.
source: In four independent biological replicates, the protein most enriched in the BAK1 complex upon CTNIP4 treatment was the LRR-RK HSL3 (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2), making this a promising candidate for being the CTNIP receptor.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data showing HSL3 enrichment in BAK1 immunoprecipitates.

claim: CTNIP induces HSL3-BAK1 complex formation.
source: We could independently confirm CTNIP-induced HSL3-BAK1 complex formation by affinity purification (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The HSL3 ectodomain can directly bind CTNIP4 with a dissociation constant of ~4 µM.
source: Consistent with a receptor function, the HSL3 ectodomain (HSL3ECD, residues 22–627) heterologously expressed in insect cells could directly bind CTNIP4 with a dissociation constant of ~4 µM in in vitro binding assays using isothermal titration calorimetry (Figure 2d–e; Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2d-e.

claim: In the presence of CTNIP4, BAK1 binds HSL3 with a dissociation constant in the sub-micromolar range (0.392 µM).
source: In the presence of CTNIP4, BAK1 bound HSL3 with a dissociation constant in the sub-micromolar range (0.392 µM) (Figure 2d–f; Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), consistent with its role as co-receptor.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data showing BAK1 binding to the HSL3-CTNIP4 complex.

claim: The two conserved cysteine residues in CTNIP4 are required for receptor binding and co-receptor recruitment.
source: Furthermore, the two conserved cysteine residues are required for receptor binding and co-receptor recruitment explaining their loss of signalling activity (Figure 2d and g–h; Figure 1—figure supplement 2c; Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data showing loss of binding when cysteines are mutated.

claim: HSL3 ectodomain does not bind IDA peptide.
source: Notably, we were unable to detect binding of INFLORESCENCE DEFICIENT IN ABSCISSION (IDA), the ligand for the related receptors HAESA and HSL2 (Meng et al., 2016; Santiago et al., 2016), to HSL3ECD (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), demonstrating distinct ligand specificity.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data showing no binding between HSL3 and IDA.

claim: IDA is the ligand for the related receptors HAESA and HSL2.
source: Notably, we were unable to detect binding of INFLORESCENCE DEFICIENT IN ABSCISSION (IDA), the ligand for the related receptors HAESA and HSL2 (Meng et al., 2016; Santiago et al., 2016), to HSL3ECD (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), demonstrating distinct ligand specificity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HSL3 lacks key conserved motifs required to recognise IDA peptides.
source: Accordingly, structural analysis of an HSL3ECD homology model reveals that the HSL3 receptor lacks key conserved motifs required to recognise IDA peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Roman et al., 2022; Santiago et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling data and citations to published literature on IDA recognition.

claim: HSL3 is phylogenetically related to HAE, HSL1, and HSL2.
source: Together, our data show that, while HSL3 is phylogenetically related to HAE, HSL1, and HSL2, it perceives distinct peptides (i.e. CTNIPs) most likely via different binding interfaces, which remains to be investigated in future structural studies.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and established knowledge of receptor relationships.

claim: HSL3 perceives distinct peptides (CTNIPs) compared to HAE, HSL1, and HSL2.
source: Together, our data show that, while HSL3 is phylogenetically related to HAE, HSL1, and HSL2, it perceives distinct peptides (i.e. CTNIPs) most likely via different binding interfaces, which remains to be investigated in future structural studies.
evidence: This is supported by binding data showing HSL3 binds CTNIPs but not IDA.

claim: HSL3 most likely perceives CTNIPs via different binding interfaces than those used by HAE/HSL1/HSL2 for IDA.
source: Together, our data show that, while HSL3 is phylogenetically related to HAE, HSL1, and HSL2, it perceives distinct peptides (i.e. CTNIPs) most likely via different binding interfaces, which remains to be investigated in future structural studies.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis showing lack of IDA-binding motifs in HSL3.

claim: HSL3 is strictly required for CTNIP-induced MAPK phosphorylation.
source: As expected, we found that HSL3 is strictly required for CTNIP-induced MAPK phosphorylation and whole genome transcriptional reprogramming (Figure 3a–b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing no MAPK phosphorylation in hsl3 mutants.

claim: HSL3 is strictly required for CTNIP-induced whole genome transcriptional reprogramming.
source: As expected, we found that HSL3 is strictly required for CTNIP-induced MAPK phosphorylation and whole genome transcriptional reprogramming (Figure 3a–b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing no differential gene expression in hsl3-1 upon CTNIP4 treatment.

claim: 30 min treatment with 100 nM CTNIP4 led to differential expression of 1074 genes in wild-type Col-0.
source: Notably, whilst 30 min treatment with 100 nM CTNIP4 led to differential expression of 1074 genes in wild-type Col-0, none were differentially expressed in hsl3-1 (p<0.05, |log2(FC)|>1) (Figure 3b; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3b and Supplementary file 3.

claim: No genes were differentially expressed in hsl3-1 upon 30 min treatment with 100 nM CTNIP4.
source: Notably, whilst 30 min treatment with 100 nM CTNIP4 led to differential expression of 1074 genes in wild-type Col-0, none were differentially expressed in hsl3-1 (p<0.05, |log2(FC)|>1) (Figure 3b; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3b and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Transient expression of HSL3 in Nicotiana benthamiana is sufficient to confer responsiveness to CTNIPs.
source: We could additionally show that transient expression of HSL3 in Nicotiana benthamiana is sufficient to confer responsiveness to CTNIPs (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by calcium influx data in N. benthamiana expressing HSL3.

claim: Plants that overexpress HSL3 become hypersensitive to active CTNIP4.
source: Furthermore, whilst 500 nM CTNIP4 was unable to significantly inhibit growth in Col-0 seedlings, plants that overexpress HSL3 became hypersensitive to active CTNIP4 (Figure 3d–e; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by seedling growth inhibition data shown in Figure 3d-e.

claim: 500 nM CTNIP4 was unable to significantly inhibit growth in Col-0 seedlings.
source: Furthermore, whilst 500 nM CTNIP4 was unable to significantly inhibit growth in Col-0 seedlings, plants that overexpress HSL3 became hypersensitive to active CTNIP4 (Figure 3d–e; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by seedling growth data shown in Figure 3d-e.

claim: CTNIPs induce general early signalling outputs indicative of RK signalling, including cytoplasmic Ca2+ influx, MAPK phosphorylation, and ROS production.
source: CTNIPs induce general early signalling outputs indicative of RK signalling, including cytoplasmic Ca2+ influx, MAPK phosphorylation, and ROS production (Figure 1; Olsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and knowledge from the literature.

claim: CTNIP4 treatment induces significant HSL3-dependent transcriptional reprogramming.
source: In addition, CTNIP4 treatment induces significant HSL3-dependent transcriptional reprogramming (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression in wild-type but not hsl3 mutants.

claim: Gene ontology analysis highlighted the enrichment of many defence- and stress-responsive pathways upon CTNIP4 treatment.
source: Consistent with the up-regulation of CTNIP and HSL3 expression by biotic elicitors (Figure 1a; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), gene ontology analysis highlighted the enrichment of many defence- and stress-responsive pathways upon CTNIP4 treatment (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: CTNIP4-induced gene expression pattern is shared with other biotic elicitors indicative of a general stress response.
source: This is a pattern shared with other biotic elicitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) indicative of a general stress response (Bjornson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of gene expression patterns and citation to published literature.

claim: Transgenic lines expressing a chimeric BIR3ecto-HSL3cyto construct exhibited developmental defects, notably enhanced root curling.
source: Transgenic lines expressing this chimeric construct exhibited developmental defects, notably enhanced root curling (Figure 3f; Figure 3—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The root curling phenotype of BIR3ecto-HSL3cyto transgenic lines is dependent upon SERK binding.
source: This phenotype is dependent upon SERK binding as the phenotype is abolished when residues essential for SERK binding are mutated (Figure 3—figure supplement 4b; Hohmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic data showing loss of phenotype in SERK-binding mutants and citation to published literature.

claim: CTNIP4 treatment inhibits root growth in an HSL3-dependent manner.
source: In addition, CTNIP4 treatment inhibited root growth and induced root skewing in an HSL3-dependent manner (Figure 3g–i; Figure 3—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: This is supported by root growth measurements shown in Figure 3g-i.

claim: CTNIP4 treatment induces root skewing in an HSL3-dependent manner.
source: In addition, CTNIP4 treatment inhibited root growth and induced root skewing in an HSL3-dependent manner (Figure 3g–i; Figure 3—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: This is supported by root angle measurements shown in Figure 3g-i.

claim: CTNIP4 overexpression is sufficient to induce root skewing and growth inhibition phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, CTNIP4 overexpression, either with or without a C-terminal tag, was sufficient to induce a similar phenotype (Figure 3j–k; Figure 3—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic data from CTNIP4 overexpression lines shown in Figure 3j-k.

claim: The HSL3-CTNIP signalling module modulates root development.
source: These data suggest that the HSL3-CTNIP signalling module modulates root development, similar to other signalling peptides recognised by LRR-RK subfamily XI members (Jeon et al., 2021; Jourquin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the root phenotype data and supported by citations to similar findings with other peptides.

claim: No difference in susceptibility to Pseudomonas syringae pv tomato DC3000 ΔAvrPto/ΔAvrPtoB was observed in hsl3 and ctnip mutant plants upon spray infection.
source: Although we initially identified CTNIPs based on their transcriptional up-regulation upon elicitor treatment, we have so far no direct evidence that they are involved in immunity, as, for example, we did not observe any difference in susceptibility of hsl3 and ctnip mutant plants to the hypovirulent Pseudomonas syringae pv tomato DC3000 ΔAvrPto/ΔAvrPtoB strain upon spray infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial infection data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: CTNIPs may be involved in the regulation of plant growth during plant-microbe interactions.
source: Although further investigation is required to test additional pathogens and conditions, it is also plausible that CTNIPs are involved in the regulation of plant growth during plant-microbe interactions – a hypothesis that needs to be tested in the future.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed root phenotypes and lack of direct immunity phenotype.

claim: HSL3 is conserved in angiosperms.
source: Recent phylogenetic analyses indicate that HSL3 is conserved in angiosperms (Figure 4a; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 16; Supplementary file 17; Supplementary file 18; Supplementary file 19; Supplementary file 20; Furumizu et al., 2021; Man et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations to published literature.

claim: CTNIPs were identified in Amborella, eudicots and monocots, excluding Poaceae.
source: CTNIPs were identified in Amborella, eudicots and monocots, excluding Poaceae (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and sequence analysis shown in Figure 4b-d.

claim: The lack of AtCTNIP4 responses in N. benthamiana suggests a co-evolution of ligand-receptor specificity.
source: Given the conservation of the HSL3-CTNIP signalling module, the lack of AtCTNIP4 responses in N. benthamiana suggests a co-evolution of ligand-receptor specificity, as for example previously proposed for PLANT ELICITOR PEPTIDE (PEP)-PEP RECEPTOR (PEPR) pairs (Huffaker, 2015; Lori et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AtCTNIP4 doesn't induce responses in N. benthamiana and supported by citations to similar findings with PEP-PEPR.

claim: Transient expression of Medicago truncatula HSL3 (MtHSL3) in N. benthamiana only induces cytoplasmic calcium influx upon treatment with a conspecific CTNIP (MtCTNIP).
source: Accordingly, transient expression of Medicago truncatula HSL3 (MtHSL3; Medtr3g110450) in N. benthamiana only induced a cytoplasmic calcium influx upon treatment with a conspecific CTNIP (MtCTNIP, Medtr1g044470) (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by calcium influx data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: No clear CTNIP could be found in Poaceae genomes.
source: Our phylogenetic analysis surprisingly revealed that no clear CTNIP could be found in Poaceae genomes (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and sequence analysis shown in Figure 4b-d.

claim: The absence of CTNIPs in Poaceae coincides with an expansion of HSL3 paralogs within these genomes.
source: Interestingly, this absence coincides with an expansion of HSL3 paralogs within these genomes (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis showing multiple HSL3 copies in Poaceae species.

claim: The HSL3-CTNIP signalling module may have diverged considerably in Poaceae.
source: We can speculate that the HSL3-CTNIP signalling module may have diverged considerably in this lineage, this may be reflected in the longer branch lengths observed in the HSL3 phylogeny, especially within the CTNIP-binding LRR domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is speculation based on phylogenetic observations of branch lengths.

claim: Over 40% of the CTNIPs identified were unannotated.
source: Interestingly, over 40% of the CTNIPs identified were unannotated, including all monocot CTNIPs (Figure 4b), highlighting how genome annotation still represents a significant challenge in the characterisation of signalling peptides.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of genome annotations shown in Figure 4b.

claim: All monocot CTNIPs identified were unannotated.
source: Interestingly, over 40% of the CTNIPs identified were unannotated, including all monocot CTNIPs (Figure 4b), highlighting how genome annotation still represents a significant challenge in the characterisation of signalling peptides.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of genome annotations shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Genome annotation represents a significant challenge in the characterisation of signalling peptides.
source: Interestingly, over 40% of the CTNIPs identified were unannotated, including all monocot CTNIPs (Figure 4b), highlighting how genome annotation still represents a significant challenge in the characterisation of signalling peptides.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many CTNIPs were not previously annotated.

claim: HSL3 has been independently identified as the CTNIP receptor (named SCREW).
source: Notably, HSL3 has been independently identified as the CTNIP receptor (there named SMALL PHYTOCYTOKINES REGULATING DEFENSE AND WATER LOSS; SCREW) (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The HSL3-CTNIP signalling module has been conserved for more than 180 million years.
source: This signalling module has been conserved for more than 180 million years (Furumizu et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2017); however, its physiological role requires additional elucidation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on angiosperm evolution.

claim: The physiological role of the HSL3-CTNIP signalling module requires additional elucidation.
source: This signalling module has been conserved for more than 180 million years (Furumizu et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2017); however, its physiological role requires additional elucidation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment that despite the findings, more work is needed to understand the biological function.

claim: HSL3 has been shown to play a role in regulating drought and disease resistance.
source: HSL3 has recently been shown to play a role in regulating drought and disease resistance implicating HSL3 in multiple stress responses (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HSL3 is implicated in multiple stress responses.
source: HSL3 has recently been shown to play a role in regulating drought and disease resistance implicating HSL3 in multiple stress responses (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies showing HSL3's role in drought and disease resistance.

claim: Deorphanising HSL3 makes LRR-RK subfamily XI an exciting tool to understand receptor-ligand co-evolution and recognition specificity.
